A.explanation: This is the $1.0 \text{ V}$ dropped across the $10 \text{ k}\Omega$ resistor, not the potential of X above the $0 \text{ V}$ wire.

B.explanation: This does not follow the $50/(10+50)$ resistance ratio for the $6.0 \text{ V}$ divider.

C.explanation: This would put most of the $6.0 \text{ V}$ drop across the lower $50 \text{ k}\Omega$ resistor, which is reversed for a divider with $0 \text{ V}$ at the bottom.

D.explanation: The potential at X is the $6.0 \text{ V}$ supply shared in the ratio $50 \text{ k}\Omega$ to $60 \text{ k}\Omega$, giving $5.0 \text{ V}$.

hints: Notice X sits between the $10 \text{ k}\Omega$ top resistor and the $50 \text{ k}\Omega$ bottom resistor, with $6.0 \text{ V}$ at the top and $0 \text{ V}$ at the bottom.
Because current in component Y is negligible, the same current flows through both resistors, so the $6.0 \text{ V}$ divides in proportion to resistance.
Compare the voltage across the $50 \text{ k}\Omega$ resistor to the total $60 \text{ k}\Omega$ to find the rise in potential from $0 \text{ V}$ up to X.
walkthrough: Identify the divider: top is $6.0 \text{ V}$, bottom is $0 \text{ V}$, upper resistance $R_1 = 10 \text{ k}\Omega$ and lower resistance $R_2 = 50 \text{ k}\Omega$, with X across $R_2$.
State the rule: with negligible current in Y, current $I$ is common, so $V_2 = I R_2$ and $V_{total} = I(R_1+R_2)$, giving $V_2 = V_{total} \times R_2/(R_1+R_2)$.
Substitute values with units: $V_X - 0 = 6.0 \text{ V} \times 50 \text{ k}\Omega/(10 \text{ k}\Omega + 50 \text{ k}\Omega)$.
Calculate the intermediate ratio: $50/60 = 5/6$, so $V_X = 6.0 \text{ V} \times 5/6 = 5.0 \text{ V}$.
Check: the larger $50 \text{ k}\Omega$ resistor takes the larger share of $6.0 \text{ V}$, so X is close to $6.0 \text{ V}$. This is option D.
